meta.title: MM-BD: Post-Training Detection of Backdoor Attacks with Arbitrary Backdoor Pattern Types Using a Maximum Margin Statistic

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers have achieved success in many research areas, but they are vulnerable to adversarial attacks . Backdoor (Trojan) attack (BA) is an important type of adversarial attack, where a classifier being attacked will predict to the attacker's target class when a test sample from one or more source classes is embedded with a backdoor pattern (BP) . A BA is typically launched by poisoning the classifier's training set with a few samples originally from the source classes, embedded with the same BP that will be used during inference, and labeled to the target class . Since successful BAs will not degrade the classifier's accuracy on test samples without the BP, they are hardly detectable, e.g. using validation set accuracy . Defenses against BAs can be deployed during the classifier's training stage to sanitize the poisoned training set , but such deployment is infeasible when the training authority is already compromised. In this paper, we consider a more practical and challenging post-training scenario, where the defender is the user of a pre-trained classifier who aims to detect whether the classifier has been backdoor attacked or not. In this scenario, the defender does not have access to the classifier's training set since it is private to the training authority or has been long forgotten. The defender also has no access to any unattacked classifiers for reference (e.g. to set a detection threshold). Existing post-training BA defenses typically assume that the defender independently possesses a small set of clean, legitimate samples from all classes in the same domain for detection. They use these samples either to reverse-engineer the BP, which is unknown to the defender, for generating statistics for anomaly detection ; or to train shallow neural networks with and without BA based on which a binary meta-classifier is trained to predict whether the classifier to be inspected is backdoor attacked or not . However, these methods heavily rely on the assumption about the BP type (and the associated embedding function) used by the attacker. For the reverse-engineering-based defenses (REDs) mentioned above, the embedding function of BP is typically involved in the reverse-engineering problem explicitly ; thus, these methods usually cannot detect BAs with other types of BP. For the methods based on meta-classification, a pool of candidate BP types is assumed for training shallow neural networks with BA ; thus, these methods may not generalize well to unseen BP types not in the training pool. Our contributions. In this paper, we propose a universal post-training backdoor defense, which, unlike other post-training defenses, does not make any assumptions about the BP type used by the attacker. Our detection method is based on the atypicality of the landscape of the classifier's output functions before softmax caused by BA. In particular, we propose a novel maximum margin (MM) statistic which is estimated using a set of random vectors for each class (solely independently of the BP type) to capture such atypicality. An unsupervised anomaly detector is then applied to the estimated MM statistics for detection inference. Thus, unlike other post-training methods, we do not need any clean legitimate samples for detection. Moreover, such design allows our method to detect BAs with arbitrary number of source classes more efficiently than many existing methods. In addition to our detector, we propose a novel BA mitigation approach in case no trustworthy classifier is available for replacement when a BA is detected. We suppress the maximum possible neuron activations using a set of optimized upper bounds (one for each neuron) without hurting the classifier's accuracy on clean test samples. To thoroughly demonstrate these advantages of our defense, we conduct experiments on four datasets for three different types of BP and a variety of training and attack configurations (e.g. different DNN architectures and different number of source classes).

sections.title: Backdoor Attack
sections.text: For a classification domain with sample space and label space , a backdoor attack (BA) aims to have the victim classifier : (a) learn to classify to the attacker's target class , when a test sample from any of the source classes is embedded with the backdoor pattern (BP); and (b) correctly classify clean test samples without BP . Typically, BAs are launched by poisoning the classifier's training set using a few samples originally from the source classes, embedded with the same BP that will be used during testing, and labeled to the target class . BA and their defense were initially proposed and intensively studied for image classification, but recently, they have also been investigated for other domains and tasks . In this paper, we focus on the image domain like most existing works; but unlike these works, our method can potentially be applicable to other domains, since it does not rely on the BP type which is usually domain dependent. For images, most popular BP types include 1) an additive perturbation embedded by , where is small (for imperceptibility) and is a clipping function ; 2) a local patch embedded using an image-wide binary mask by , where is small for imperceptibility and represents element-wise multiplication ; and 3) a local or global pattern blended using an image-wide binary mask and a blending factor by , where is close to 0 for imperceptibility. Other more recent BP types include a reflection-based BP that mimics physical reflection on smooth surfaces , a wrapping-based BP that introduces a spatial transformation to existing pixels , and a BP embedded in the frequency domain of images .

sections.title: Backdoor Defense
sections.text: Defenses against BA can be deployed during the classifier's training stage to detect backdoor poisoning and sanitize the poisoned training set if a detection is made . However, these defenses are not applicable to scenarios where the defender is a downstream user who has no access to the training process. In this paper, we consider a popular post-training scenario where the defender aims to detect whether a pre-trained classifier is backdoor attacked or not, but has no access to the classifier's training set or any clean classifiers for reference. In a similar scenario considered by , the main goal is to detect if a test samples is embedded with a BP, thus is not in the scope of this paper. Existing methods detecting BAs post-training include a family of meta-learning approaches. A large number of shallow neural networks labeled with attacked or not attacked are trained features extracted from these labeled networks are then used to train a binary meta-classifier for BA detection . However, these methods assume a pool of candidate BP types that may be used by the attacker. They may fail when the actual BP type used by the attacker is not in the pool. Moreover, training the shallow networks requires a relatively large number of clean samples and is timely inefficient. Another family of reverse-engineering-based defenses (REDs) trial reverse-engineer the BP for each putative target class, hoping to recover the actual BP used by the attacker for the true target class if there is a BA . Such BP reverse-engineering is performed on a small set of clean samples independently possessed by the defender , or on simulated samples obtained by model inversion . Detection inference is then performed on the statistics obtained from the estimated BPs (e.g. the norm of the estimated mask for patch replacement BP) the classifier is deemed to be attacked if there exists an abnormal statistic. However, REDs rely on assumptions about the BP type since the BP estimation process requires direct involvement of the BP embedding function. Also, most REDs require an independent clean dataset for detection, which is not always available in practice. In comparison, our universal detector does not make any assumptions about the BP type, and does not need any clean legitimate samples for detection. Moreover, most REDs fail when the BA involves only few source classes. addressed this issue by estimating a pattern for each class pair, but the computational cost increases dramatically. While and focused on estimation of the BA source classes along with the target class by proposing a complicated optimization procedure, our method is born out with the ability to detect BAs with arbitrary number of source classes with high time efficiency, as will be shown in our experiments. Once a BA is detected, a secondary goal is to mitigate the attack when there are no classifiers for replacement. In , the classifier deemed to be attacked is fine-tuned on a relatively large number of clean samples to unlearn the backdoor mapping. Although the main focus of this paper is BA detection, in Sec. , we additionally propose a method that effectively mitigates BA with most types of BPs using very few clean samples and without fine-tuning any of the classifier's original parameters. Our method can also be enhanced by existing ones to achieve even better performance.

sections.title: Method
sections.text: Again, we focus on the image domain and the post-training defense scenario where the defender has no access to the classifier's training set or any clean classifiers for reference. More importantly, we do not make any assumptions about the BP type or the number of source classes involved in the BA. We first discuss the key ideas behind our detection method in Sec. . Then, in Sec. , we present our detection procedure which consists of an estimation step to obtain a novel maximum margin (MM) statistic for each class, followed by an unsupervised detection inference step. Additionally, we propose an approach to mitigate detected BAs in Sec. .

sections.title: Key Ideas
sections.text: Our detector is based on the influence of BA on the landscape of the classifier's logit (i.e. the output before softmax) functions independently of the BP type. Consider a BA with target class and denote the classifier's logit function associated with any class as (assuming compact without loss of generality). Regardless of the BP type, we will likely observe: for any class . That is, if we find for each class the MM between its logit and the second largest logit, the MM for the true BA target class will be much larger than for all other classes. Why BA causes the above phenomenon? Note that BP is a common pattern selected by the attacker to be embedded in all samples used for poisoning the classifier's training set; and the same BP will be embedded in test samples to induce test-time misclassification. In contrast, class discriminant features typically exhibit high variability e.g., bird of different species, or even the same object captured into an image with different views, distances, or lighting conditions. The commonality of BP is important for it to override discriminant features of source class samples they are embedded in such that it can be easily learned (at a low poisoning rate ) by the victim classifier during training. However, the repetition of the common BP in the training set also induces an inevitable overfitting, which boosts the target class logit (by causing abnormally large activations to neurons positively correlated with this logit) while depressing the logits of other classes. sections.title: Detection Procedure
sections.text: Estimation step. For each putative target class , we estimate a MM statistic by solving: using gradient ascent with projection onto (e.g. for color images with height , width , and channel ) until convergence (which is guaranteed for continuous logit functions and compact ). As a common practice, we consider multiple random initialization in (e.g., for images, pixel values are uniformly randomly initialized in ), and pick the best optimal solution. Compared with REDs that perform BP estimation with presumed embedding function, our optimization problem is independent of the BP type. Moreover, since samples not from any source classes may not be (mis)classified to the target class even when the true BP is embedded, REDs' BP estimation using clean samples from all non-target classes may fail when the majority of these classes are not source classes. In contrast, our method is capable to detect BAs with arbitrary number of source classes, since problem () above does not involve any clean legitimate samples. Detection inference step. We propose an unsupervised anomaly detector inspired by . Denote the estimated MM statistic for each class as and the largest statistic as . We hypothesize that, when there is a BA, will be associated with the BA target class and will be an outlier to the distribution of MM statistics for non-target classes. Thus, we estimate a null distribution using all statistics excluding . Given that MM is strictly positive (both theoretically and empirically for estimated MM in our experiments), we consider single-tailed density forms for the null distribution, e.g. a Gamma distribution in our experiments. To evaluate the atypicality of under the estimated null, we compute an order statistic p-value like in : where is the total number of classes in the domain. It can be easily shown that follows a uniform distribution on under the null hypothesis of no attack. Thus, we claim a detection with confidence (e.g. with the classical ) if . If a BA is detected, the class associated with is inferred as the BA target class.

sections.title: Mitigation of Backdoor Attack
sections.text: When a BA is detected, the victim classifier can be replaced by a new one from another trustworthy training authority; otherwise, prediction made by the victim classifier to classes other than the detected BA target class can still be trusted. However, an alternative choice is to mitigate the backdoor attack. Our mitigation approach is based on the observation that BA induces a subset of neurons in each layer to have an abnormally large activation (which is accumulated layer by layer, resulting in a large MM for the BA target class). Such large activation phenomenon is also the basis of the BA detection approach in , though several hyperparameters are required, e.g., to select neurons responsible for the large activation. In contrast, we apply to each neuron a specific optimized upper bound (without selection) to suppress any possible large activation caused by BA, without significant degradation on the classifier's accuracy on clean samples. sections.title: Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments are conducted mainly on four benchmark datasets with different image resolution, image size and number of classes: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 , TinyImageNet, and GTSRB . Details of these datasets are deferred to Apdx. XXX.

sections.title: Main Experiments for Backdoor Attack Detection
sections.text: In the following, we show the effectiveness of our universal backdoor detector, dubbed UnivBD, in terms of detection accuracy and efficiency compared with several state-of-the-art post-training backdoor detectors for a variety of BA configurations (e.g. BP type, number of source classes). sections.title: Settings
sections.text: We consider three common BP types in the BA literature: additive perturbation, patch replacement, and blending (with associated embedding functions in Sec. ). For the additive perturbation BP, we consider a global chessboard pattern from and a local pixel perturbation from . For the patch replacement BP, we consider a noisy patch from and a unicolor patch from . For the blended BP, we consider a blended noisy patch from . For convenience, we denote the above five BPs as A1-A5 respectively. For A2, the pixel being perturbed is randomly selected and fixed for each attack; for A3-A5, both the color and the location of the patch are randomly selected and fixed for each attack. Examples of these five BPs are shown in Fig. , with more details in Apdx. XXX. Like most existing works (e.g. ), we consider BAs with one target class (which is randomly selected for each attack). However, we allow BAs to have one or multiple source classes for brevity, these two source class settings are denoted as `S' (for single) and `M' (for multiple) respectively. For each BA with the `S' setting, the source class is randomly selected. For TinyImageNet, we randomly select ten source classes for each BA with the `M' setting; while for the other three datasets, all classes other than the target class are selected as the source classes (which is assumed by the detectors in ) for the `M' setting. With the above notations, a BA with chessboard BP and multiple source classes is denoted as `A1-M'. For CIFAR-10, we create ten ensembles of BAs for all ten combinations of A1-A5 and `S'/`M' respectively. For CIFAR-100 and GTSRB, we create five BA ensembles for A1-A5 respectively, all with the `M' setting. We do not create BAs with a single source class for these two datasets because we cannot generate sufficient backdoor training images to launch a successful BA, given limited number of clean images in each class of these two datasets. For TinyImageNet, we only generate one BA ensemble with the setting `A3-M' (which is arbitrarily selected) since the amount of time to just train a classifier on this dataset is extraordinarily high. For each ensemble, ten different BAs are generated independently according to the specified settings using the classical data poisoning protocol in . Other configurations including the number of backdoor training images created for BAs in each ensemble are deferred to Apdx. XXX. We train one classifier for each BA we created. The DNN architectures for BAs on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and GTSRB are ResNet-18 , VGG-16 , ResNet-34 , and MobileNet , respectively. Training configurations are detailed in Apdx. XXX. For each dataset, we also create an ensemble of ten clean classifiers to evaluate the false detection rate. All the BAs we created are successful with high attack success rate (ASR) and negligible degradation in clean test accuracy (ACC) compared with the clean classifiers trained for the same dataset (see Apdx. XXX).

Detection accuracy. In Tab. , we show the detection accuracy of our UnivBD compared with the other methods on the BA ensembles we created and the number of legitimate images used by each method for each dataset. We also show the proportion of clean classifiers deemed to be not attacked by each detector. We only evaluate PTRED and META for CIFAR-10 since the empirical computational cost applying these two methods to BAs on the other datasets are overly high. Also due to the time constraint (and the space limitation), we include detection accuracy results for a few arbitrarily selected BA ensembles for CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and GTSRB, respectively. Complete results for our UnivBD for all BA ensembles are shown in Apdx. XXX. As we have discussed in Sec. , existing post-training BA detectors presume one or several BP types. For example, NC shows strong capability in detecting BAs with patch replacement BPs (A3A4) it is designed for; but NC fails to detect BAs with local perturbation BP (A2). Similar results are reported for ABS and META, which are designed for patch BPs (A3-A5), while not addressing additive perturbation BPs (A1A2). In contrast, PTRED performs well for additive perturbation BPs (A1A2) it is designed for, but is generally ineffective for the other BP types (A3-A5). TABOR and TND do not show competitive performance compared with the other methods, since they adopt additional constraints on the shape or color of the BP more discussions are deferred to Apdx. XXX. Different with all these methods, our UnivBD achieves high detection accuracy for all BP types (A1-A5) with low false detection rate for all datasets, thus is invariant of the BP type. Even if ABS (effective for patch BPs A3-A5) and PTRED (effective for additive perturbation BPs A1-A2) are jointly deployed, the detection accuracy on classifiers with BA is just comparable to the our UnivRED, but with more false detections and significant increment in computational cost. Moreover, NC, TABOR, ABS, and TND assume that BA has multiple source classes (i.e. with the `M' setting), thus they are generally less effective for BAs with singles source class (i.e. with the `S' setting). However, our UnivBD is generally invariant to the number of source classes involved in the BA as shown in Tab. , since UnivBD does not make any assumptions about the number of source classes. Finally, different with all other methods, our UnivBD does not need any legitimate images for detection.
